questions.question: What type of relationship does inheritance represent between a child class and a parent class?
options: A "has-a" relationship (e.g., a Car has-a Engine)
An "is-a" relationship (e.g., a Dog is-a Animal)
A "uses-a" relationship (e.g., a Programmer uses-a Computer)
A "contains-a" relationship (e.g., a Library contains-a Book)
questions.explanation: Inheritance creates an "is-a" relationship. The child class is a more specific version of the parent class. A Dog is a specific type of Animal, so Dog inherits from Animal.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax to create a class called `Poodle` that inherits from a class called `Dog`?
options: `class Poodle extends Dog:`
`class Poodle(Dog):`
`class Poodle inherits Dog:`
`class Poodle < Dog:`
questions.explanation: In Python, inheritance is specified by placing the parent class name in parentheses after the child class name: `class Child(Parent):`.

options: It will cause an error because Cat doesn't have an eat method
It will print "Eating..." because Cat inherits the eat method from Animal
It will print "Meow!" because that's Cat's only method
It will do nothing because eat wasn't defined in Cat
questions.explanation: Child classes inherit all methods from their parent class. Since Cat inherits from Animal, it automatically gets the `eat()` method, even though it's not explicitly defined in Cat.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of calling `super().__init__()` in a child class constructor?
options: To delete the parent class attributes
To ensure the parent class's constructor runs and initializes inherited attributes
To create a new instance of the parent class
To prevent the child class from accessing parent methods
questions.explanation: When a child class defines its own `__init__`, the parent's `__init__` is not automatically called. `super().__init__()` explicitly calls the parent constructor to initialize inherited attributes.

options: `parent.__init__(color)`
`Vehicle.__init__(color)`
`super().__init__(color)`
`__init__(color)`
questions.explanation: The correct syntax in Python 3 is `super().__init__(color)`. This calls the parent class's `__init__` method and passes the required arguments.

questions.question: What will happen if a child class defines its own `__init__` method but DOES NOT call `super().__init__()`?
options: The parent class's `__init__` will still run automatically
The program will crash immediately with a syntax error
The parent class's `__init__` will NOT run, and inherited attributes may not be initialized
Python will create a default constructor automatically
questions.explanation: When a child defines its own `__init__`, it overrides the parent's constructor. The parent's `__init__` is not called automatically, so any initialization code in the parent (like setting attributes) will not execute unless explicitly called with `super()`.

questions.question: What is method overriding in Python?
options: Defining multiple methods with the same name but different parameters
Redefining a method in a child class that already exists in the parent class
Calling a method from the parent class using super()
Preventing a method from being accessed outside the class
questions.explanation: Method overriding occurs when a child class provides its own implementation of a method that is already defined in its parent class. The child's version 'overrides' the parent's version.

questions.question:
Why does the following code demonstrate polymorphism?

```python
def make_sound(animal):
    print(animal.sound())

make_sound(Dog())
make_sound(Cat())
```
options: Because Dog and Cat are different classes
Because the function works with any object that has a sound() method, regardless of its class
Because the function only works with Animal objects
Because it uses the super() function
questions.explanation: This demonstrates polymorphism because the `make_sound()` function doesn't care what type of object it receives - it only cares that the object has a `sound()` method. Different objects can respond to the same method call in their own way.

questions.question: What happens if you try to instantiate an Abstract Base Class (ABC) directly?
options: It creates an empty object
It raises a TypeError
It creates the object but with None values
It automatically creates a default child class
questions.explanation: Abstract Base Classes cannot be instantiated directly. Python raises a TypeError because they are designed only to be inherited from, not used directly.

questions.question: What happens if a child class inherits from an ABC but fails to implement one of its abstract methods?
options: The child class will still work, but the method will raise an error when called
The child class will also become abstract and cannot be instantiated
Python will automatically provide a default implementation
The program will crash at import time
questions.explanation: If a child class doesn't implement all abstract methods from its parent ABC, it also becomes an abstract class and cannot be instantiated. Python will raise a TypeError when you try to create an instance.

questions.question: What is the correct way to import what's needed for abstract classes?
options: `from abc import abstract`
`from abc import ABCMeta`
`from abc import ABC, abstractmethod`
`from interfaces import ABC`
questions.explanation: Import `ABC` (the base class) and `abstractmethod` (the decorator) from the `abc` module. Your abstract class inherits from `ABC`, and abstract methods use `@abstractmethod`.
